purpose: machine-facing planning/evaluation ontology of concrete home-server and self-hosting work-units (hardware, storage/RAID, OS, containers/services, networking, remote access, security, and ops) for a knowledge-searcher meta-KB; supports prioritization, dependency analysis, conflict resolution, risk control, validation, and session-bounded execution.
assumptions: single-household / small home-lab scale, not enterprise multi-site
no observed dataset supplied; all numeric values are heuristic priors
operator is a technically capable hobbyist sysadmin, not a 24/7 ops team
Linux/NAS-OS and containerized services are the default substrate
internet access exists but a static public IP is not assumed (CGNAT possible)
exclusions: enterprise datacenter, multi-tenant, or hyperscale cloud operations
deep application-internal development of the hosted apps themselves
physical building/electrical work beyond UPS and basic power protection
regulated-data compliance regimes (HIPAA/PCI) beyond general good practice

competency_questions.question: what should the home server do, for whom, and under what budget/power/uptime constraints?
what hardware platform and base OS fit the requirements and capacity targets?
what storage layout and redundancy level should protect the data on this hardware?
how is data protected against failure, corruption, and power loss beyond redundancy?
how are hosts, services, and names addressed and resolved on the network?
how are self-hosted applications deployed reproducibly and reached over encrypted connections?
how is the network segmented and firewalled so only intended services are reachable?
how is remote access provided securely, and when (if ever) is public exposure justified?
what is the deliberate public attack surface and how is each exposed endpoint hardened?
how are credentials, identities, and access controlled across the stack?
can the system actually be recovered, and is recovery documented and tested?
how is the running system observed, and how is capacity/lifecycle managed over time?
how are updates, hardening, and documentation kept current without breaking services?

glossary.definition: running applications and services on hardware you own and control rather than on third-party SaaS
combining disks for redundancy or performance so the array survives a bounded number of disk failures
three copies of data, on two media types, with one off-site copy
a server that terminates TLS and routes inbound requests by hostname to backend services
the automated protocol (e.g. Let's Encrypt) for issuing and renewing TLS certificates
an encrypted tunnel that lets authenticated remote clients reach internal services without public exposure
a router rule that maps a public WAN port to an internal host, exposing it to the internet
splitting the LAN into isolated segments so a compromise in one cannot reach another
a firewall posture that blocks all inbound traffic except explicitly allowed flows
an isolated, reproducible package of an app and its dependencies run by a container runtime
recovery time objective and recovery point objective: how fast and to what data freshness recovery must reach
an orderly automated shutdown on power loss that flushes writes and exports pools to avoid corruption

evidence_label_policy.note: No observed/experimental inputs supplied; only heuristic labels are eligible.

source_registry.description: Heuristic priors from established home-server and Linux system-administration practice (Upton & Halfacree, Raspberry Pi User Guide; Nemeth et al., UNIX and Linux System Administration Handbook) and common self-hosting community practice; no measured dataset supplied.
grounding_limits: all numeric values are heuristic priors, not measurements
no observed or experimentally_validated labels are eligible

nodes.definition: Define what the home server must do, target services, users, uptime expectations, and constraints before any hardware or software choice.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a new workload class (e.g. GPU transcoding) is introduced

pros.claim: prevents rework by fixing scope before purchase
pros.example: writing down 'Jellyfin 4 transcodes + Nextcloud 3 users' sizes CPU/RAM up front

cons.claim: over-spec wastes budget and power
cons.example: buying a 64GB Xeon for a DNS-only box

failure_modes: scope creep into untracked services
ignored power/noise/heat limits
acceptance_tests: requirements cover every planned service and named user
capacity targets are numeric and testable
revisit_triggers: household usage grows past capacity target

nodes.definition: Choose the server/NAS hardware platform (SBC like Raspberry Pi, mini-PC, repurposed desktop, or NAS appliance) sized to requirements.

included: SBC vs x86 vs NAS appliance

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a chosen platform reaches EOL or cannot meet revised capacity

pros.claim: matching platform to workload avoids premature replacement
pros.example: Pi 5 fits low-power services; mini-PC fits transcoding

cons.claim: hardware is semi-irreversible once bought
cons.example: wrong NAS bay count blocks future drive expansion

failure_modes: underpowered platform forces early replacement
ARM/x86 arch mismatch with needed software
revisit_triggers: platform EOL or thermal throttling observed

nodes.definition: Design the storage layout: disk count/sizes, RAID/ZFS/mdadm level, filesystem, and redundancy vs capacity tradeoff.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a disk fails, is replaced, or pool fill crosses the redundancy threshold

pros.claim: ZFS/btrfs checksumming detects silent corruption RAID alone misses
pros.example: monthly scrub flags a failing drive before total loss

cons.claim: RAID is not a backup and rebuilds are risky
cons.example: RAID5 rebuild on large disks can hit a second URE and lose the array

failure_modes: RAID treated as backup; data lost on dual failure or ransomware
silent bit-rot on non-checksumming filesystem
rebuild stress kills a second aging disk
acceptance_tests: chosen RAID level survives the documented disk-failure tolerance
scrub/resilver completes without unrecoverable errors
usable capacity meets target after redundancy overhead

nodes.definition: Install and baseline the server OS (Linux distro/NAS OS), set up users, SSH, time, locale, and an automatic-update posture.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the distro nears end-of-life or an update breaks a driver

pros.claim: key-only SSH and a non-root admin user shrink the attack surface immediately
pros.example: disabling PasswordAuthentication stops brute-force logins

cons.claim: aggressive auto-updates can break running services
cons.example: an unattended kernel bump dropped a NIC driver mid-session

failure_modes: password SSH left enabled
root login over network
no NTP causing cert/log skew

nodes.definition: Install and configure the container runtime (Docker/Podman) and compose tooling as the standard service-deployment substrate.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a container-escape or image-supply-chain advisory is published

pros.claim: containers give reproducible, isolated, easily-backed-up services
pros.example: compose file fully describes a service stack for redeploy

cons.claim: Docker publishes ports bypassing UFW/firewalld by default
cons.example: a container reachable on 0.0.0.0 despite a host firewall deny rule

failure_modes: rootful Docker bypasses host firewall via published ports
unpinned :latest tags cause drift
leftover dangling images fill disk
revisit_triggers: new app needs unsupported runtime feature

nodes.definition: Deploy individual self-hosted applications (media, files, dashboards, automation) as containers/services with persistent volumes.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: an app ships a breaking major version or new app joins the stack

pros.claim: persistent volumes + compose make apps reproducible and portable
pros.example: moving a volume dir migrates Nextcloud to new hardware intact

cons.claim: each app adds update, backup, and exposure surface
cons.example: ten apps means ten changelogs and CVE feeds to track

failure_modes: data stored in ephemeral container layer and lost on recreate
unpinned image breaks on update
port collisions between apps

nodes.definition: Front services with a reverse proxy (Nginx/Caddy/Traefik) terminating TLS and routing by hostname for unified, encrypted access.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a new public hostname is added or ACME renewal automation changes

pros.claim: single TLS-terminating entrypoint centralizes certs and access policy
pros.example: Caddy auto-issues and renews Let's Encrypt certs per host

cons.claim: the proxy is a single point of failure and a high-value target
cons.example: a proxy misconfig can expose every backend app at once

failure_modes: expired/failed ACME renewal breaks all HTTPS access
misrouted hostname exposes admin UI
weak TLS ciphers enabled

nodes.definition: Establish internal name resolution and addressing: static IPs/DHCP reservations, local DNS, and a naming scheme for hosts and services.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a new host needs a name or the DHCP/static range layout changes

pros.claim: stable names and reservations make every downstream config durable
pros.example: reverse proxy and certs reference names, not fragile IPs

cons.claim: a single local resolver is a LAN-wide dependency
cons.example: Pi-hole down means clients lose DNS unless a fallback exists

failure_modes: IP conflict from overlapping DHCP and static ranges
stale DNS cache routes to old host
single resolver outage breaks all name lookups

nodes.definition: Define host and network firewall policy and segmentation (VLANs/subnets) to limit lateral movement and expose only intended services.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a new exposed port, device class, or segment is introduced

pros.claim: default-deny + segmentation contains a single compromised device
pros.example: an infected smart bulb on its VLAN cannot touch the file server

cons.claim: over-tight rules silently break service-to-service traffic
cons.example: blocking inter-VLAN mDNS broke casting until explicitly allowed

failure_modes: Docker-published ports bypass the host firewall
over-broad allow rule exposes admin services
flat network lets a compromised IoT device reach the NAS
acceptance_tests: default-deny inbound is enforced and only intended ports are reachable
IoT/guest segment cannot reach the server management plane
revisit_triggers: new service needs a port opened
new device class joins the network

nodes.definition: Provide secure remote access to home services via VPN (WireGuard/Tailscale) or an authenticated tunnel, avoiding broad port exposure.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a remote client is added/lost or the home's public-exposure model changes

pros.claim: VPN keeps services off the public internet while enabling remote use
pros.example: WireGuard peer reaches Nextcloud without any port forward

cons.claim: key management and peer revocation are easy to neglect
cons.example: a lost laptop with an un-revoked key retains LAN access

failure_modes: forwarding raw ports instead of a VPN exposes services to the internet
leaked WireGuard key grants full LAN access
full-tunnel misconfig breaks client internet
acceptance_tests: only authenticated VPN peers can reach internal services
no admin service is directly reachable from the public internet

nodes.definition: Decide and implement any deliberate public exposure (port forward, tunnel like Cloudflared, dynamic DNS) with hardening for what must be reachable.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: any new endpoint becomes publicly reachable or abuse traffic rises

pros.claim: a reverse tunnel exposes one service without opening router ports
pros.example: Cloudflared publishes a single app while the WAN stays closed

cons.claim: any public ingress is continuously scanned and attacked
cons.example: an exposed Plex login saw credential-stuffing within hours

failure_modes: accidental exposure of an admin port
dynamic DNS revealing home IP to abuse
no rate limiting on a public login
acceptance_tests: every publicly reachable endpoint is enumerated and intentionally hardened
no management/admin interface is published to the internet
revisit_triggers: a new endpoint is exposed publicly

nodes.definition: Store and inject service credentials, API keys, and certs securely, keeping them out of compose files, images, and version control.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a secret is suspected leaked or a new credentialed service is added

pros.claim: centralized secret injection enables rotation and least-exposure
pros.example: a leaked key is rotated in one place, not across ten compose files

cons.claim: a single secret store is a high-value single point of compromise
cons.example: root access to the host can read the injected environment of every app

failure_modes: secrets committed to a public/private git repo
secrets baked into image layers
no rotation after staff/device change
acceptance_tests: no plaintext secret appears in images, compose files, or git history
credential rotation is possible without rebuilding images

nodes.definition: Manage user accounts, authentication (MFA/SSO), and per-service authorization across the self-hosted stack.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a user joins/leaves or an app without native auth is exposed

pros.claim: forward-auth/SSO adds MFA in front of apps that lack it
pros.example: Authelia gates a no-auth dashboard behind 2FA

cons.claim: centralized auth (SSO) outage can lock out every protected service
cons.example: an Authelia failure blocked all apps until bypassed

failure_modes: one shared admin account with no MFA
app with no auth published behind only a guessed path
stale accounts of departed users
acceptance_tests: admin actions require MFA and are not on a shared account
each user has least-privilege access to only their services

nodes.definition: Design backups with the 3-2-1 rule: scheduled, versioned, off-box (and offsite) copies of data and configs, independent of RAID.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the data layout changes or a backup job starts failing

pros.claim: off-box versioned backups survive hardware loss and ransomware
pros.example: restic to a remote bucket recovers data after a total NAS failure

cons.claim: backups consume bandwidth, storage, and ongoing verification effort
cons.example: unverified backups give false confidence until a failed restore

failure_modes: only on-box backups lost with the host or to ransomware
silent backup-job failures unnoticed for months
no encryption on offsite copies
acceptance_tests: at least one off-box copy exists and is verified to differ from primary
a versioned backup can recover a file deleted weeks ago

nodes.definition: Periodically validate that backups actually restore and that the system can be rebuilt within an acceptable recovery objective.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: backup tooling changes or a recovery objective is revised

pros.claim: a periodic test restore converts hope into a verified recovery capability
pros.example: a quarterly restore drill caught a corrupt backup chain early

cons.claim: DR drills take time and can disrupt running services if careless
cons.example: a careless restore test overwrote live data once

failure_modes: backups that never actually restore
recovery depends on undocumented tribal knowledge
RTO far exceeds tolerance under real failure
acceptance_tests: a full restore of a critical dataset succeeds within the target RTO
the runbook lets a rebuild proceed without tacit knowledge

nodes.definition: Collect health, capacity, and security signals (uptime, disk/SMART, logs) and alert on conditions that need action.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a new service is added or alert signal-to-noise degrades

pros.claim: proactive alerts catch disk-full and failing disks before outage
pros.example: an 85% pool-fill alert prevented a write-failure cascade

cons.claim: noisy or misconfigured alerts cause fatigue and missed real events
cons.example: a chatty alert channel trained the admin to ignore it

failure_modes: disk fills with no warning and crashes services
alert fatigue causes a real failure to be ignored
no alerting so failures found by users

nodes.definition: Maintain a controlled patch cadence for OS, containers, and apps balancing security currency against stability and breakage risk.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a critical CVE affects a deployed component or an update causes breakage

pros.claim: a snapshot-before-update policy makes patches safely reversible
pros.example: a btrfs/ZFS snapshot let a broken kernel update roll back in minutes

cons.claim: patching can introduce regressions and downtime
cons.example: a Docker image bump changed a config schema and broke the app

failure_modes: unpatched exposed service exploited
an update breaks a service with no rollback
auto-update applied during peak use
acceptance_tests: security patches for exposed services land within the defined window
every update has a tested rollback or snapshot to revert to
revisit_triggers: critical CVE for a deployed component

nodes.definition: Protect against power loss with a UPS and automated graceful shutdown to prevent filesystem and pool corruption.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the UPS fails self-test or the protected load grows

pros.claim: graceful shutdown on power loss prevents pool/FS corruption
pros.example: NUT shut the server down cleanly during a 20-minute outage

cons.claim: UPS batteries degrade and give false safety if untested
cons.example: an unverified UPS battery died instantly during an outage

failure_modes: abrupt power loss corrupts a write or pool
UPS present but no automated shutdown configured
aged UPS battery fails under load

nodes.definition: Maintain configuration-as-record, runbooks, and a change log so the system is reproducible and recoverable without tacit knowledge.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the topology changes or another operator must take over

pros.claim: config-as-record makes rebuilds and handoffs reproducible
pros.example: a documented compose repo rebuilt the whole stack on new hardware

cons.claim: docs rot quickly and create false confidence when stale
cons.example: a runbook referenced a removed service and misled recovery

failure_modes: recovery blocked by undocumented setup
drift between docs and live config
single-person knowledge silo
revisit_triggers: a service or topology change occurs

nodes.definition: Apply a cross-cutting hardening baseline (least privilege, attack-surface reduction, fail2ban, audit) reconciling all security controls.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a new exposure/control is added or a relevant advisory is published

pros.claim: a unifying baseline catches gaps no single control owns
pros.example: a surface review found an app still bound to 0.0.0.0

cons.claim: over-hardening can break legitimate access and usability
cons.example: an aggressive fail2ban locked out the admin's own IP

failure_modes: controls drift apart leaving an unintended gap
hardening one layer while another stays default
no intrusion mitigation on exposed logins
acceptance_tests: the exposed attack surface matches the documented intended surface
brute-force/abuse mitigation is active on every exposed auth endpoint
revisit_triggers: a new exposure or control is introduced
a security advisory affects the stack

nodes.definition: Periodically review capacity growth, hardware/disk aging, and service lifecycle to plan upgrades and decommissioning before failure.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a capacity trend or hardware-age threshold is crossed

pros.claim: trend-based review pre-empts capacity and aging failures
pros.example: a fill-rate trend triggered a disk upgrade two months before full

cons.claim: forecasts can over- or under-provision against real growth
cons.example: an over-cautious upgrade doubled cost for unused capacity

failure_modes: pool fills before an upgrade is planned
aged disks fail in clusters
retired service left running and exposed
revisit_triggers: a disk passes its expected service life

edges.why_related: requirements size the platform
edges.risk_of_conflict: skipping it oversizes/undersizes hardware
edges.example: Pi-only DNS vs transcoding mini-PC follow from the service list
edges.resolution_rule: requirements dominate; revise hardware if scope changes

edges.why_related: bay/controller count bounds the RAID layout
edges.risk_of_conflict: RAID design built before hardware causes layout rework
edges.example: a 2-bay NAS cannot host the intended RAIDZ2 pool
edges.resolution_rule: hardware constraints dominate the RAID level choice

edges.why_related: architecture (ARM/x86) determines OS/image choice
edges.risk_of_conflict: installing wrong-arch image wastes a cycle
edges.example: Pi needs an ARM image; mini-PC needs x86
edges.resolution_rule: hardware arch dominates OS image selection

edges.why_related: the base OS hosts the container runtime
edges.benefit_of_coupling: runtime installs on a stable base
edges.risk_of_conflict: runtime on an unhardened OS inherits weaknesses
edges.example: Docker installed after SSH-key hardening on Debian
edges.resolution_rule: OS baseline must be set before runtime install

edges.why_related: host networking config underpins naming/addressing
edges.benefit_of_coupling: stable names build on a configured host
edges.risk_of_conflict: naming before host config drifts
edges.example: static IP set on the host before DNS records reference it
edges.resolution_rule: host network config precedes naming

edges.why_related: apps deploy onto the runtime
edges.risk_of_conflict: deploying apps before a stable runtime causes redo
edges.example: compose stacks run only after Docker is configured
edges.resolution_rule: runtime readiness gates app deployment

edges.why_related: the proxy fronts deployed apps
edges.benefit_of_coupling: unified TLS entry for all apps
edges.risk_of_conflict: proxy config before apps know their ports thrashes
edges.example: Traefik routes to a Nextcloud container by service name
edges.resolution_rule: apps and their ports must exist before proxy routing finalizes

edges.why_related: hostnames resolve the proxy's routes and cert names
edges.risk_of_conflict: missing names break vhost routing and ACME
edges.example: cloud.home.lan must resolve before Caddy issues its cert
edges.resolution_rule: name resolution precedes proxy hostname routing

edges.why_related: addressing/segments are the basis for firewall rules
edges.risk_of_conflict: rules before addressing reference wrong ranges
edges.example: an IoT VLAN subnet must exist before a deny rule cites it
edges.resolution_rule: addressing/segmentation plan precedes firewall rule authoring

edges.why_related: VPN ingress is admitted by firewall policy
edges.benefit_of_coupling: remote access fits the segmentation model
edges.risk_of_conflict: VPN before firewall opens uncontrolled paths
edges.example: WireGuard's UDP port is the only inbound allow on the WAN
edges.resolution_rule: firewall policy must admit the VPN before remote access is enabled

edges.why_related: prefer VPN before choosing any public exposure
edges.benefit_of_coupling: exposure decided only after VPN exists
edges.risk_of_conflict: exposing services before a VPN exists invites unnecessary risk
edges.example: decide a public tunnel only after WireGuard covers most needs
edges.resolution_rule: default to VPN; require justification before any public ingress

edges.why_related: public ingress routes through the TLS proxy
edges.benefit_of_coupling: one hardened TLS entrypoint for exposure
edges.risk_of_conflict: exposing apps directly bypasses TLS/routing controls
edges.example: Cloudflared forwards to the proxy, not raw app ports
edges.resolution_rule: public ingress must traverse the reverse proxy

edges.why_related: the runtime injects secrets into services
edges.risk_of_conflict: baking secrets in images before a store leaks them
edges.example: Docker secrets / env-file injection instead of hardcoded keys
edges.resolution_rule: secret injection mechanism precedes crediting apps

edges.why_related: auth systems consume managed credentials/keys
edges.risk_of_conflict: auth before secrets store hardcodes credentials
edges.example: Authelia's secrets come from the store, not plaintext config
edges.resolution_rule: secrets management underpins identity/auth configuration

edges.why_related: apps are the subjects of access control
edges.risk_of_conflict: auth designed before apps exist misses real surfaces
edges.example: forward-auth wraps each deployed app that lacks native login
edges.resolution_rule: deployed apps define what access control must cover

edges.why_related: backups protect data the storage layer holds
edges.risk_of_conflict: treating RAID as backup skips real protection
edges.example: restic copies the ZFS dataset off-box nightly
edges.resolution_rule: backups are required regardless of RAID; RAID is not a backup

edges.why_related: app data/volumes are backup targets
edges.risk_of_conflict: backing up before volumes are mapped misses data
edges.example: the Nextcloud data volume is added to the backup set
edges.resolution_rule: app persistent volumes define the backup scope

edges.why_related: restore testing validates the backups
edges.risk_of_conflict: skipping tests leaves backups unverified
edges.example: a quarterly restore of the backup set into a scratch VM
edges.resolution_rule: a backup is not trusted until a restore test passes

edges.why_related: running services are what monitoring observes
edges.risk_of_conflict: monitoring before services exist has nothing to watch
edges.example: uptime and disk checks target the deployed stack
edges.resolution_rule: deployed services define monitoring targets

edges.why_related: storage health drives capacity/SMART alerts
edges.risk_of_conflict: unmonitored pools fail silently
edges.example: SMART and pool-fill alerts come from the storage layer
edges.resolution_rule: storage signals feed monitoring; alert thresholds follow capacity plan

edges.why_related: the patch policy maintains the installed OS
edges.risk_of_conflict: patching policy without a base OS is moot
edges.example: unattended-upgrades posture set at install, refined into policy
edges.resolution_rule: the installed OS is the object of patch management

edges.why_related: app updates are a core patch surface
edges.risk_of_conflict: unmanaged app updates break stacks
edges.example: an image bump is staged with a snapshot rollback ready
edges.resolution_rule: apps need a patch+rollback policy, not ad-hoc :latest pulls

edges.why_related: graceful shutdown protects pool integrity on power loss
edges.benefit_of_coupling: no corruption from abrupt power loss
edges.risk_of_conflict: a pool without UPS shutdown risks corruption
edges.example: NUT triggers a clean ZFS export before the UPS dies
edges.resolution_rule: storage integrity needs power-loss protection

edges.why_related: monitoring detects post-update regressions
edges.risk_of_conflict: silent regressions persist without monitoring
edges.example: an error-rate spike after an update triggers rollback
edges.resolution_rule: trigger: post-update anomaly; stop: metrics back to baseline or rolled back

edges.why_related: monitoring trends feed capacity/lifecycle planning
edges.risk_of_conflict: planning without trend data guesses
edges.example: fill-rate trend drives a disk-upgrade decision
edges.resolution_rule: monitoring data is the input to lifecycle review

edges.why_related: DR drills produce the recovery runbook
edges.risk_of_conflict: undocumented recovery depends on memory
edges.example: the restore drill is written up as a step-by-step runbook
edges.resolution_rule: DR testing must yield documented runbooks

edges.why_related: network/firewall config must be recorded to be maintainable
edges.risk_of_conflict: undocumented rules cause drift
edges.example: the VLAN/firewall map is captured in the network diagram
edges.resolution_rule: security topology must be documented

edges.why_related: firewall policy is a pillar of the hardening baseline
edges.risk_of_conflict: a baseline without firewall input is incomplete
edges.example: the surface review confirms only intended ports are open
edges.resolution_rule: firewall posture feeds the hardening baseline

edges.why_related: identity/auth posture is part of the baseline
edges.risk_of_conflict: gaps where apps lack auth
edges.example: the baseline flags any exposed app without MFA
edges.resolution_rule: identity coverage feeds the hardening baseline

edges.why_related: exposed surface is the focus of hardening
edges.risk_of_conflict: unintended exposure persists
edges.example: every public endpoint is enumerated and hardened in the review
edges.resolution_rule: exposure inventory feeds the hardening baseline

edges.why_related: patch currency is a hardening dimension
edges.risk_of_conflict: an unpatched exposed service undermines hardening
edges.example: the review confirms exposed services are within the patch window
edges.resolution_rule: patch posture feeds the hardening baseline

edges.why_related: redundancy goals push hardware cost/bays beyond budget
edges.risk_of_conflict: over-spec for redundancy blows the budget
edges.example: RAIDZ2 wants 6 bays but the chosen mini-PC has 2
edges.resolution_rule: cap redundancy to the budgeted platform unless data sensitivity justifies more bays

edges.why_related: convenient public access opposes default-deny exposure minimization
edges.risk_of_conflict: exposure widens the surface segmentation tried to shrink
edges.example: publishing an app fights the default-deny firewall posture
edges.resolution_rule: security (minimize surface) dominates unless a documented need + hardening justify exposure

edges.why_related: patch currency opposes service stability/uptime
edges.benefit_of_coupling: balances security currency against breakage risk
edges.risk_of_conflict: aggressive updates break running services
edges.example: an auto image bump broke a running app's config schema
edges.resolution_rule: stage updates with a tested rollback; security patches for exposed services still win

edges.why_related: locking access behind VPN opposes frictionless usability
edges.risk_of_conflict: VPN-only access frustrates casual users
edges.example: family members must connect WireGuard before reaching the media app
edges.resolution_rule: prefer VPN for admin/sensitive services; allow hardened public access only for low-risk apps

edges.why_related: RAID-as-backup belief opposes real off-box backup effort
edges.risk_of_conflict: relying on RAID skips real backups
edges.example: a user skips backups believing RAIDZ2 is enough
edges.resolution_rule: backups are mandatory; redundancy never substitutes for an off-box copy

edges.why_related: tight hardening opposes app functionality/usability
edges.risk_of_conflict: over-hardening breaks legitimate app features
edges.example: a strict CSP/fail2ban policy blocked a legitimate app feature
edges.resolution_rule: relax the minimum needed for function while preserving the security objective; document exceptions

edges.why_related: both govern how external clients reach internal services
edges.risk_of_conflict: conflating them muddles the exposure decision
edges.example: both answer 'how do I reach my server from outside?'
edges.resolution_rule: keep distinct: VPN = private tunnel; ingress = deliberate public surface

conflict_axes.trigger: desired fault tolerance exceeds the budgeted bays/drives
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: data sensitivity sets a floor on redundancy; cost caps the ceiling; raise budget only for high-sensitivity data
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: redundancy floor for critical data cannot be met within budget
conflict_axes.example: RAIDZ2 desired but only a 2-bay box is funded

conflict_axes.trigger: a desired feature needs public reachability
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: default-deny dominates; public exposure allowed only with documented need plus hardening (TLS, auth, rate-limit)
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: exposing an admin/management interface is requested
conflict_axes.example: forwarding the router admin port to the internet

conflict_axes.trigger: a security update risks breaking a running service
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: security patches for exposed/high-severity items win; cosmetic updates defer; always keep a rollback
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: a critical CVE patch may break a production app
conflict_axes.example: a kernel CVE fix risks a NIC driver regression

conflict_axes.trigger: a hardening control blocks a legitimate workflow
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: preserve the security objective but relax the minimum needed for function; document every exception
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: fail2ban or CSP blocks a real user action
conflict_axes.example: strict 2FA frustrates a shared household media account

conflict_axes.trigger: users want access without installing/connecting a VPN
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: VPN dominates for admin and sensitive data; hardened public ingress allowed only for low-risk read services
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: family wants the media app reachable without WireGuard
conflict_axes.example: casual photo sharing vs admin dashboard exposure

conflict_axes.trigger: redundancy is mistaken for a backup, deprioritizing off-box copies
resolution_order: state that RAID is availability not backup
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: off-box versioned backup is mandatory and never substituted by RAID; redundancy only improves availability
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: a user skips backups trusting RAIDZ2
conflict_axes.example: ransomware encrypts the array and the only copy

conflict_axes.trigger: fully automatic updates apply changes with no human checkpoint
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: automate low-risk reversible updates; require human review for irreversible or exposure-changing updates
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: auto-applying a major version bump unattended
conflict_axes.example: an unattended OS upgrade changed firewall defaults

conflict_axes.trigger: adding more services raises the patch/monitor/backup burden
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: add a service only if its value exceeds its ongoing patch/backup/monitor cost; prefer consolidation
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: running 20 niche apps overwhelms update tracking
conflict_axes.example: each new app adds a CVE feed and a backup target

conflict_axes.trigger: centralizing proxy/DNS/auth creates a stack-wide dependency
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: centralize for manageability but add a documented fallback for any component whose outage blocks the whole stack
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: Pi-hole DNS or the SSO provider going down breaks everything
conflict_axes.example: an Authelia outage locks every protected app

edge_cases.trigger: redundancy deployed but no off-box backup exists
edge_cases.failure_mode: total data loss on dual failure or ransomware
edge_cases.example: RAIDZ2 array with zero off-box copies
edge_cases.detection_method: check backup inventory for an off-box, versioned target distinct from the array

edge_cases.trigger: a published container port is reachable despite a host firewall deny
edge_cases.failure_mode: unintended exposure of an internal service
edge_cases.example: an app on 0.0.0.0:8080 reachable from the LAN despite UFW deny
edge_cases.detection_method: scan from another host for ports the firewall claims to block
resolution: bind containers to localhost or an internal network
route external access only via the proxy

edge_cases.trigger: automatic TLS certificate renewal silently fails
edge_cases.failure_mode: expired cert breaks HTTPS to all services
edge_cases.example: Let's Encrypt renewal blocked by a closed port-80 challenge
edge_cases.detection_method: monitor cert expiry dates and renewal job exit status

edge_cases.trigger: a credential is committed to a git repo or baked into an image
edge_cases.example: an API token pushed in a compose file or .env to a repo
edge_cases.detection_method: scan repos/images for secret patterns; review .gitignore
resolution: move it to the secret store

edge_cases.trigger: backups run but are never test-restored
edge_cases.failure_mode: unrecoverable data when a real restore is attempted
edge_cases.example: a corrupt or incomplete backup chain discovered only during an incident
edge_cases.detection_method: perform a periodic test restore into a scratch environment

edge_cases.trigger: raw ports forwarded to the internet instead of using a VPN
edge_cases.example: SSH or a DB port forwarded on the router to reach it remotely
edge_cases.detection_method: audit router port-forward rules against the exposure inventory
resolution: route access via VPN or a hardened tunnel

edge_cases.trigger: UPS present but no automated graceful shutdown configured
edge_cases.failure_mode: pool/filesystem corruption on a long outage
edge_cases.example: the UPS holds power but the server still hard-powers-off when it dies
edge_cases.detection_method: test a simulated power-loss and confirm clean shutdown

edge_cases.trigger: an update is applied with no snapshot or rollback path
edge_cases.failure_mode: prolonged outage when an update breaks a service
edge_cases.example: a :latest image pull changes a config schema with no way back
edge_cases.detection_method: verify a snapshot/pinned-prior-version exists before each update

edge_cases.trigger: untrusted IoT/guest devices share the server's flat network
edge_cases.failure_mode: a compromised device reaches the management plane
edge_cases.example: a smart bulb on the same subnet can reach the NAS admin UI
edge_cases.detection_method: map device classes to segments and test cross-segment reachability

edge_cases.trigger: the only local DNS resolver fails
edge_cases.failure_mode: LAN-wide name resolution outage breaks services
edge_cases.example: Pi-hole down leaves clients unable to resolve any name
edge_cases.detection_method: check for a configured secondary/fallback resolver
resolution: add a secondary resolver or upstream fallback
set client DNS to include the fallback

edge_cases.trigger: system recovery depends on undocumented tribal knowledge
edge_cases.failure_mode: recovery stalls or fails when the operator is unavailable
edge_cases.example: no runbook exists to rebuild the stack on new hardware
edge_cases.detection_method: attempt a rebuild using only the documentation and note gaps

workflow.objective: fix scope, capacity targets, and the hardware platform
acceptance_tests: requirements cover every named service and user
platform meets capacity targets

handoff_artifact.required_contents: requirements document; capacity targets; selected platform spec

workflow.do_first_because: scope and hardware are the most irreversible upstream decisions everything depends on

workflow.objective: lay down storage redundancy and a hardened base OS
acceptance_tests: pool survives the documented failure tolerance
root SSH and password auth are disabled

handoff_artifact.required_contents: storage layout spec; pool config; base OS config record

workflow.do_first_because: storage redundancy and OS baseline are high-irreversibility foundations for every service

workflow.objective: establish stable addressing, names, segmentation, and default-deny firewall
entry_criteria: base OS is installed and on the network
acceptance_tests: only intended ports are reachable
IoT/guest cannot reach management plane

handoff_artifact.required_contents: IP/hostname plan; DNS records; firewall ruleset; segmentation map

workflow.do_first_because: stable naming and a default-deny network are prerequisites for safe service exposure

workflow.objective: stand up the container runtime, deploy apps with persistent volumes, and inject secrets safely
entry_criteria: base OS and network are stable
acceptance_tests: apps reproducible from compose
secrets injected, not hardcoded

handoff_artifact.required_contents: compose project; volume map; secret-injection mechanism

workflow.do_first_because: services depend on a stable runtime and must consume managed secrets from creation

workflow.objective: front services with TLS routing and enforce authentication/authorization
entry_criteria: apps are deployed and names resolve
acceptance_tests: each app routed by hostname over TLS
no shared admin account without MFA

handoff_artifact.required_contents: routing map; TLS certs; identity/auth policy

workflow.do_first_because: encrypted access and auth must wrap services before any remote or public reachability is enabled

workflow.objective: enable secure remote access via VPN and make any public exposure deliberate and hardened
entry_criteria: firewall and TLS/auth are in place
gates: only authenticated peers reach internal services
acceptance_tests: VPN works for remote clients
every public endpoint is enumerated and hardened
exit_criteria: remote access defined and exposure recorded

handoff_artifact.required_contents: VPN config; peer inventory; public exposure decision record

workflow.do_first_because: remote access must build on firewall + TLS and prefer VPN over broad public exposure

workflow.objective: protect data with 3-2-1 backups, validate restores, and add power-loss protection
gates: an off-box copy exists and verifies
a test restore succeeds within RTO
acceptance_tests: 3-2-1 satisfied
restore proven
graceful shutdown tested

handoff_artifact.required_contents: backup policy; offsite copy proof; restore test report; UPS config

workflow.do_first_because: backups and proven restore are non-negotiable before trusting the system with real data

workflow.objective: add monitoring/alerting and a controlled, reversible patch cadence
entry_criteria: services are running and backed up
acceptance_tests: actionable alerts configured
patch window and rollback defined

handoff_artifact.required_contents: monitoring stack; alert rules; patch+rollback policy

workflow.do_first_because: you cannot safely operate or patch what you cannot observe and cannot roll back

workflow.objective: reconcile all security controls into a baseline and capture config/runbooks
entry_criteria: network, access, exposure, and patching exist
acceptance_tests: no unintended exposure
docs let another operator recover the system

handoff_artifact.required_contents: hardening baseline; surface review; system documentation; runbooks

workflow.do_first_because: the cross-cutting baseline catches gaps no single control owns; docs make it maintainable

workflow.objective: establish periodic capacity, aging, and lifecycle review to pre-empt failures
gates: capacity trends are tracked against thresholds
acceptance_tests: upgrade/retire decisions are scheduled before failure
exit_criteria: a recurring review cadence is running
workflow.do_first_because: trend-based review converts day-to-day signals into proactive upgrade and decommission planning

dominance_rules.trigger: an irreversible or data-loss-risking step could be rushed
dominance_rules.rule: data-integrity and irreversibility risk dominate delivery speed
dominance_rules.required_action: stop and apply the safety control before proceeding
dominance_rules.example: never skip backups to ship a service faster

dominance_rules.trigger: a high-value node has unmet prerequisites
dominance_rules.rule: true dependency precedence dominates raw value ordering
dominance_rules.example: do not expose services publicly before the firewall and TLS exist

dominance_rules.trigger: redundancy is offered as a backup substitute
dominance_rules.rule: an off-box versioned backup is mandatory and never replaced by RAID
dominance_rules.required_action: create and verify an off-box backup
dominance_rules.example: RAIDZ2 does not exempt the system from a 3-2-1 backup

dominance_rules.rule: default-deny and minimal surface dominate convenience exposure
dominance_rules.required_action: prefer VPN; allow public ingress only with documented need + hardening
override_requires: documented exposure decision and hardening evidence
dominance_rules.example: do not forward an admin port to gain convenience

dominance_rules.trigger: a high-severity CVE affects an exposed service
dominance_rules.rule: security patches for exposed/high-severity items dominate short-term uptime
dominance_rules.required_action: patch within the window with a rollback ready
dominance_rules.example: patch an internet-facing RCE even at the cost of a maintenance window

dominance_rules.trigger: backups exist but were never restored
dominance_rules.rule: a proven restore dominates an assumed-good backup
dominance_rules.required_action: run a test restore before trusting the backup
dominance_rules.example: a backup is not 'done' until a restore succeeds

dominance_rules.trigger: an irreversible or exposure-changing update is queued
dominance_rules.rule: human review dominates automation for irreversible or exposure-changing actions
dominance_rules.required_action: require a human checkpoint before applying
dominance_rules.example: do not auto-apply a major OS upgrade that changes firewall defaults

dominance_rules.trigger: a shared admin account is proposed for ease
dominance_rules.rule: least-privilege and per-user MFA dominate the convenience of shared accounts
dominance_rules.required_action: provision per-user least-privilege access with MFA
override_requires: documented exception for a constrained service account
dominance_rules.example: replace a shared root login with per-user keys and MFA

dominance_rules.trigger: power loss threatens an active write
dominance_rules.rule: graceful shutdown to protect data dominates squeezing extra runtime
dominance_rules.required_action: trigger automated shutdown at the holdover threshold
dominance_rules.example: shut down cleanly before the UPS dies rather than risk pool corruption

dominance_rules.rule: documented, reproducible procedure dominates undocumented tribal knowledge
dominance_rules.required_action: capture the config and runbook before locking the step
override_requires: temporary exception with a follow-up doc task
dominance_rules.example: write the rebuild runbook so anyone can recover the stack

anti_rework_rules.rule: fix requirements and capacity before buying hardware
anti_rework_rules.rationale: hardware is semi-irreversible; wrong sizing forces costly replacement
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a platform purchased before the service list is known
anti_rework_rules.example: buying a 2-bay NAS then needing a 6-disk pool

anti_rework_rules.rule: select hardware before designing the RAID/pool layout
anti_rework_rules.rationale: bay/controller count bounds feasible RAID layouts
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a RAIDZ2 design that the chosen chassis cannot hold

anti_rework_rules.rule: harden the base OS before deploying services
blocked_until: base OS hardened (key-only SSH, non-root admin)
anti_rework_rules.rationale: services on an unhardened OS inherit its weaknesses and need redo
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: apps deployed while password SSH is still open
anti_rework_rules.example: exposing apps on a box still allowing root password login

anti_rework_rules.rule: establish addressing, names, and default-deny firewall before any exposure
anti_rework_rules.rationale: exposing services on an unsegmented, unfiltered network multiplies attack surface
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a port forwarded before the firewall is default-deny
anti_rework_rules.example: forwarding a port on a flat network

anti_rework_rules.rule: stand up secret injection before crediting apps
anti_rework_rules.rationale: secrets hardcoded early leak into images and git history
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: an API key committed in a compose file
anti_rework_rules.example: a token baked into an image layer

anti_rework_rules.rule: prefer and stand up VPN before considering public exposure
blocked_until: VPN access exists and covers admin/sensitive services
anti_rework_rules.rationale: public exposure decided without a VPN option defaults to unnecessary risk
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: raw port forwarding chosen before WireGuard was tried
anti_rework_rules.example: forwarding SSH instead of using a tunnel

anti_rework_rules.rule: create and verify off-box backups before trusting the system with real data
blocked_until: off-box backup exists and a test restore passed
anti_rework_rules.rationale: loading real data onto an unbacked system risks unrecoverable loss
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: production data on a host with only on-box copies
anti_rework_rules.example: migrating photos before any off-box backup exists

anti_rework_rules.rule: prove a restore before treating data protection as done
blocked_until: a test restore has succeeded within RTO
anti_rework_rules.rationale: unverified backups create false confidence and silent unrecoverability
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a backup job green but never restored
anti_rework_rules.example: discovering a corrupt chain during a real incident

anti_rework_rules.rule: add monitoring before relying on the system in production
blocked_until: capacity and disk-health alerts are active
anti_rework_rules.rationale: operating blind lets disk-full and failing disks become outages
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a full disk crashing services with no prior alert
anti_rework_rules.example: SMART failures unnoticed until total loss

anti_rework_rules.rule: document config and runbooks before locking or handing off the system
anti_rework_rules.rationale: undocumented systems cannot be reproduced, recovered, or handed off
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a hardening baseline with no record of what was changed
anti_rework_rules.example: recovery blocked because setup lived only in memory

iteration_protocol.trigger: a validator or acceptance test fails
iteration_protocol.detection: validator exit code != 0 or a failed check
acceptance_tests: every failed check is mapped to a cause

action: rank defects by risk and blast radius
acceptance_tests: high-risk defects are addressed before cosmetic ones
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: queue is empty or only sub-threshold defects remain

iteration_protocol.trigger: a change touches a high-coupling or locked component
iteration_protocol.detection: change targets a node with X>=0.75 or soft/hard lock
acceptance_tests: all downstream dependents are identified

iteration_protocol.trigger: a defect is assigned for repair
action: route the defect to its repair owner subsystem
acceptance_tests: the targeted check now passes

iteration_protocol.detection: an applied repair exists since last validation
acceptance_tests: no new failures were introduced

iteration_protocol.trigger: new evidence about a node's importance arrives
action: recompute affected metrics with the small formula script
acceptance_tests: recomputed scores match the formulas within tolerance

iteration_protocol.detection: a change request targets a soft/hard-locked node
action: downgrade the lock with impact analysis
acceptance_tests: the change is revalidated and re-locked

iteration_protocol.trigger: risk or irreversibility crosses a review threshold
iteration_protocol.detection: risk_score high or human_review_required node changes
action: escalate to a human reviewer with a decision record
acceptance_tests: a documented human decision exists before proceeding
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: human sign-off recorded or change abandoned

NAS with RAIDZ2 and no backups

expected_properties: security patch dominates uptime with rollback

change_triggers: new service or workload class added
security advisory affecting a deployed component
version_increment_rules: increment on any change to a soft/hard-locked node
increment when exposure or storage layout changes
